prompt:
# Reconstruct a principle card from a citation

You are given **a citation and nothing else**. Reconstruct, from your own
knowledge of that document, the principle card a human extractor would have
written after reading it.

This is not a request to design something. It is a request to report what a
specific paper says. If you do not know the paper, say so — an honest "I do not
know this document" is a **correct** answer here and is more useful than a
plausible reconstruction.

## The citation

<!-- ---- CITATION BLOCK BEGIN ---- -->
Etienne, A. S. & Jeffery, K. J. (2004). "Path integration in mammals." Hippocampus 14(2), 180-192.
<!-- ---- CITATION BLOCK END ---- -->

## The system the principle has to fit

The card is for a Unitree Go2 quadruped navigating an indoor space it has no map
of. Below it sits an inherited, pretrained, **frozen** locomotion policy: the
only thing anything ever sends the robot is a Twist — `(vx, vy, wz)`. Sensing is
a 181-beam planar lidar, an odometry-based pose estimate that drifts, and a goal
that may or may not have been disclosed.

## What a card is

Six fields. `mechanism`, `trigger` and `derivation` are prose. `prediction` is
**structured**, because a prediction that cannot be decided automatically cannot
become a unit test.

```yaml
id: <short_snake_case_identifier>
node_name: <TheLeafThisWouldProduce>       # CamelCase, verb-first

source:
  citation: <the citation you were given, verbatim>
  span: <the section, page, figure or equation number where the mechanism is
         stated — the part that makes a threshold checkable. LEAVE EMPTY if you
         are not confident of the location.>

mechanism: <what the finding says happens, and why it helps>
trigger: <the condition under which it applies>
derivation: <how that becomes a rule for this robot and these sensors>

prediction:
  statement: <the falsifiable claim, in words>
  metric: <one of: goal_reached, spl, collisions, near_misses, min_clearance,
           stuck_events, recovery_time, localisation_failures, time_to_goal>
  baseline: <goal_seeker or reactive_avoid>
  min_effect: <a number: the smallest effect that would count as support>
  cost_metric: <the metric this mechanism is expected to make WORSE>

confidence: <high | medium | low>
```

`confidence` has written criteria and they are about **the source**, not about
how sure you feel:

- **high** — the mechanism *and* its quantitative form are stated explicitly in
  the document; you can point at the equation, threshold or exponent itself.
- **medium** — the mechanism is stated explicitly, but the quantitative form is
  adapted. The number is yours; the mechanism is theirs.
- **low** — the mechanism is described qualitatively and the derivation is
  yours. Still usable, but it is your claim wearing their citation.

## What to return

One fenced ```yaml block containing exactly one card, and nothing else that
looks like YAML. Prose outside the fence.

**Two things this probe is measuring, so answer them honestly rather than
completely:**

1. **Do not invent a `span`.** An empty span is a result. A section number you
   are reconstructing from the shape of such papers is the exact failure this
   exists to detect, and it will be checked against the document.
2. **Do not invent numbers.** If the paper states a threshold, an exponent or a
   closed form, give it. If it does not, say the derivation is yours and set
   `confidence: low`. A number you are not certain came from this paper is worse
   than no number.

response.text:
I know this paper — it is Etienne & Jeffery's review of mammalian path integration in the 2004 *Hippocampus* special issue, covering the idiothetic (vestibular, proprioceptive, motor-efference, optic-flow) updating of a homing vector, the cumulative error that makes it unusable over long unaided excursions, and the periodic recalibration of that vector by familiar allothetic cues — including the cue-conflict result that a small landmark/PI discrepancy is absorbed by the landmarks while a large one is rejected in favour of the internal estimate. What I do **not** have reliably is where in the paper each of those is stated (section heading, page, figure), and I do not have a specific numeric mismatch threshold that I can attribute to *this* review rather than to the primary hamster and head-direction-cell literature it summarises. So: `span` empty, thresholds mine, `confidence: low`.

```yaml
id: bounded_reset_of_dead_reckoned_pose
node_name: ResetPoseOnTrustedLandmarkMatch

source:
  citation: 'Etienne, A. S. & Jeffery, K. J. (2004). "Path integration in mammals." Hippocampus 14(2), 180-192.'
  span: ""

mechanism: >
  Mammals continuously integrate self-motion signals (vestibular, proprioceptive,
  motor efference copy, optic flow) into a single vector pointing back to a
  reference location, and can home on that vector with no external cues at all.
  The integration is open-loop, so error — especially in the directional
  component, which the head-direction system carries — accumulates monotonically
  with distance and with each turn, and an uncorrected estimate degrades to
  uselessness over a long excursion. The review's central point is that path
  integration is therefore not a standalone navigation system but one half of a
  loop: familiar allothetic cues periodically reset the integrator, and the
  integrator in turn carries the animal between cue encounters and disambiguates
  cues that look alike. Crucially the reset is not unconditional. In cue-conflict
  experiments a modest discrepancy between the landmark-specified direction and
  the internally computed one is resolved in favour of the landmarks (the
  integrator is recalibrated); a large discrepancy is resolved in favour of the
  internal estimate, and the landmark is treated as having moved rather than the
  animal as having erred. This asymmetry is what keeps a corrupt external match
  from destroying an otherwise good internal estimate.
trigger: >
  Applies during travel through space with no reliable global fix, whenever a
  previously visited configuration is re-encountered and the dead-reckoned pose
  disagrees with it. Not applicable on the first traverse of unseen space (no
  stored reference to match against), nor when drift is still small enough that
  the two estimates agree.
derivation: >
  The Go2 has exactly the Etienne–Jeffery ingredients: an idiothetic estimator
  (wheel/IMU odometry integrated through the frozen locomotion policy, drifting)
  and an allothetic channel (the 181-beam planar scan). Give the robot a homing
  vector maintained from the Twist commands and odometry, and store a small ring
  of scan signatures (range-histogram plus principal wall directions) at places
  it has been. On re-observing a stored signature, compute the pose correction
  it implies. Apply the correction only if it is bounded — my numbers, not the
  paper's: heading correction under 45 deg and translation under 1.0 m are
  accepted and the integrator is snapped to the landmark estimate; anything
  larger is rejected as a false match and the dead-reckoned pose is retained,
  with the offending signature demoted rather than trusted. The 45 deg figure is
  chosen to mirror the qualitative small-vs-large asymmetry the review describes,
  not because the review states it. Between accepted resets the robot navigates
  purely on the integrated vector, so the mechanism costs nothing when no match
  is available.
prediction:
  statement: >
    A Go2 that dead-reckons a homing vector and resets it against stored lidar
    signatures only when the implied correction is small will suffer fewer
    localisation failures over a multi-room indoor traverse than a goal_seeker
    that trusts odometry alone, and — separately — fewer than one that accepts
    every landmark match unconditionally, because unbounded acceptance lets a
    single aliased corridor match teleport the pose estimate.
  metric: localisation_failures
  baseline: goal_seeker
  min_effect: 0.30
  cost_metric: time_to_goal
confidence: low
```
